Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Acts 16, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## Acts 16 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Paul meets Timothy at Lystra

**Traditional Reading:** Paul (with Silas) revisits Derbe and Lystra, cities where he had previously planted churches on the first missionary journey about five years earlier (Barclay's estimate). He finds Timothy, already a "disciple" — almost certainly converted during Paul's earlier visit, since Paul later calls him "my true child in the faith" (1 Tim. 1:2). Timothy's mother Eunice was a believing Jewess; his father was a Greek Gentile, probably an unbeliever (the term "believer" is applied only to the mother in the Greek). The name Timothy (Timotheos) means "one who honours God."
— enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, studylight.org (Gill), studylight.org (Ellicott)

### v. 2 — Timothy's good reputation

**Traditional Reading:** Timothy was "well spoken of" by the brethren not only in his hometown Lystra but also in Iconium, some distance away. This indicates he had already been active in ministry, travelling between the churches. For a young man (perhaps 18–20; Ellicott notes Paul still speaks of his "youth" twelve years later in 1 Tim. 4:12), this wide reputation was remarkable.
— studylight.org (Gill), studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com

### v. 3 — Paul circumcises Timothy

**Traditional Reading:** This is one of the most discussed verses in the chapter. Paul had just come from the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), where it was decided circumcision was *not* required for salvation. He was literally carrying that decree to the churches. Yet he circumcises Timothy. The traditional explanation is consistent across all the older commentaries:

- **It was not for salvation** but for practical ministry access. Uncircumcised, Timothy (son of a Jewish mother) would be regarded by Jews as an apostate Jew and barred from synagogues.
- **Contrast with Titus** (Gal. 2:3): Titus was a full Gentile; Paul refused to circumcise him because it was being demanded as necessary for salvation. Timothy was half-Jewish; Paul circumcised him voluntarily for the sake of the mission.
- **Paul's principle**: "to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews" (1 Cor. 9:20). The wording "he took him and circumcised him" implies Paul himself performed it.
- Gill adds: under Jewish law, a woman could not circumcise, which is why Timothy had remained uncircumcised despite his Jewish mother.
— enduringword.com (quoting Bruce, Longenecker, Hughes), studylight.org (Gill), studylight.org (Ellicott)

**Denominational Differences:** Not a major point of division between Protestant traditions. All agree Paul was not compromising on justification by faith.

### vv. 4–5 — Delivering the Jerusalem decree; churches strengthened

**Traditional Reading:** As they travelled, Paul and his team delivered "the decrees" (dogmata) — the letter from the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:23–29) containing four directives for Gentile believers: abstain from idol-food, blood, strangled animals, and sexual immorality. The result was twofold: churches were "strengthened in the faith" (internal health) and "increased in number daily" (external growth). Gill notes that strong doctrine and unified practice produced both stability and growth.
— studylight.org (Gill), preceptaustin.org, enduringword.com

### v. 6 — Forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach in Asia

**Traditional Reading:** "Asia" here means the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today), with Ephesus as its chief city. Paul naturally wanted to go there, but the Holy Spirit "forbade" them. The means of this prohibition is not specified — possibly an inward impulse, a prophetic word, or circumstances. Gill suggests it was "a secret and powerful impulse upon their minds." God's reasons were hidden in His sovereign will; Gill adds it was "because at this instant, there were no chosen ones to be called by grace, and there was work for the apostle…elsewhere, namely, in Macedonia."
— studylight.org (Gill), enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org

### v. 7 — The Spirit of Jesus prevents entry into Bithynia

**Traditional Reading:** After being blocked from Asia, they tried to go north into Bithynia (along the Black Sea coast), but again the Spirit prevented them. The better manuscripts read "the Spirit of Jesus" rather than simply "the Spirit." Ellicott notes this is "of some dogmatic importance, as confirming the doctrine that the Spirit stands in the same relation to the Son as to the Father, and may therefore be spoken of either as the Spirit of God, or of Christ (Rom. 8:9), or of Jesus."
— studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com

### v. 8 — Passing by Mysia to Troas

**Traditional Reading:** Shut out of both Asia and Bithynia, they "passed by" (or "passed through without stopping") Mysia and arrived at Troas, a Roman colony and free city on the Aegean coast. They had been guided by closed doors to exactly where God wanted them.
— studylight.org (Gill), enduringword.com

### vv. 9–10 — The Macedonian vision; "we" begins

**Traditional Reading:** At Troas, Paul received a night vision of a "man of Macedonia" pleading, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." This was the divine explanation for all the closed doors: God was calling the gospel westward into Europe for the first time. The missionaries "immediately" sought passage. The sudden shift from "they" to "we" in v. 10 is almost universally taken to mean that Luke (the author) joined the team at Troas. Ellicott suggests Luke may have been the founder of the church at Troas and had been labouring there before Paul arrived. Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that God's "no" to Asia and Bithynia also served to give Paul a personal physician (Luke) and to give the church the man who would write more of the New Testament than anyone else.
— enduringword.com, studylight.org (Ellicott), studylight.org (Gill)

### vv. 11–12 — Arrival at Philippi

**Traditional Reading:** With favourable winds ("a straight course"), they sailed via Samothrace to Neapolis (modern Kavalla), then travelled inland to Philippi. Luke describes Philippi as "the leading city of that district of Macedonia" (or "a first city of the border-country," as Ellicott translates more precisely) and a Roman "colony." A Roman *colonia* was a military settlement whose citizens possessed full Roman rights — it was legally an extension of Rome itself. Philippi had been re-founded by Augustus after the battle of 42 BC.
— studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com

### v. 13 — The place of prayer by the river

**Traditional Reading:** On the Sabbath, finding no synagogue in Philippi (a synagogue required ten Jewish men; Bruce notes that "no number of women would compensate for the absence of even one man"), they went outside the city gate to the riverside where a *proseuchē* (place of prayer) was customarily located. Jewish communities without a synagogue often met by water for ritual ablutions. They found only women gathered. Ellicott notes that Juvenal's *Satires* reference these Jewish riverside oratories. Paul and his team sat down (the posture of teachers) and spoke to them.
— studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com (quoting Bruce)

### v. 14 — Lydia's conversion: "The Lord opened her heart"

**Traditional Reading:** Lydia was a "seller of purple" (luxury dyed cloth) from Thyatira, a city famous for its dyeing guilds. She was a "worshiper of God" (a Gentile proselyte to Judaism). The key phrase is "The Lord opened her heart to respond (or 'to give heed') to the things spoken by Paul." 

**Denominational Differences — This is a major theological fault line:**

- **Reformed / Calvinist reading:** This verse is a clear demonstration of monergistic regeneration — God must sovereignly open the heart before anyone can believe. Guzik (Enduring Word, broadly Reformed-Baptist): "This is a work God must do in all who believe, because as Jesus said, no one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him (John 6:44)." Prayer for God to open hearts is therefore the essential element in evangelism. The Ligonier article on Reformed baptism similarly emphasizes that the Spirit works regeneration sovereignly, not automatically through the sacrament.
  — enduringword.com, ligonier.org

- **Wesleyan / Arminian reading:** While affirming that the Lord must open the heart, Wesleyan teachers stress that Lydia was already a "worshiper of God" seeking truth, and God's opening of her heart was a response to her seeking — prevenient grace enabling, but not compelling, her free response. (Specific Wesleyan site not accessed; this is the well-known traditional distinction.)

- **Lutheran reading:** Lutherans would affirm that God opens the heart through the Word — the means of grace. The Spirit works through the preached Word to create faith. Baptism (see v. 15) would also be seen as a means by which God confers grace.
  — 1517.org (article on Lutheran vs Reformed assurance)

— studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com

### v. 15 — Baptism of Lydia and her household

**Traditional Reading:** Lydia and "her household" were baptised. She then prevailed upon the missionaries to stay at her house — evidence of immediate fruit in hospitality.

**Denominational Differences — Household baptism and infant baptism:**

- **Baptist reading:** The "household" does not prove infant baptism. Lydia may have been unmarried (she is named as the business owner, not her husband), and her "household" likely consisted of servants and employees. All who were baptised had heard and believed (see v. 32 for the jailer's household parallel). John MacArthur (GTY) notes that baptism in Acts consistently follows faith, never precedes it.
  — gty.org

- **Reformed / Presbyterian reading:** Household baptisms in Acts (Lydia, the jailer, Crispus, Stephanas) are part of the covenantal argument for infant baptism. While this passage alone doesn't *prove* infants were present, it is consistent with the Old Testament pattern of household solidarity in covenant signs (circumcision). The Westminster Confession teaches baptism as a sign and seal of covenant promises, not regeneration *ex opere operato*.
  — ligonier.org

- **Lutheran reading:** Baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe this" (Luther's Small Catechism). Lutherans would see this household baptism as a means of grace through which God conferred saving benefits — though faith must receive it. The tension with *sola fide* that some Reformed critics note (see TGC article) is resolved by Lutherans through the understanding that baptism itself creates and nourishes faith.
  — 1517.org, thegospelcoalition.org

- **Anglican:** The 1662 Book of Common Prayer retains the baptismal regeneration language ("this Child is regenerate") while also insisting on personal faith. Anglican views range from a Reformed covenantal understanding to a more Catholic sacramental view, with the 39 Articles affirming baptism as "a sign of regeneration."
  (No specific Anglican page accessed.)

- **Catholic / Orthodox:** Both teach baptismal regeneration — baptism actually washes away original sin and confers grace *ex opere operato*. The household baptism would include all members, including infants.
  — (catholic.com, oca.org pages not accessed in this search)

### vv. 16–17 — The slave girl with a Python spirit

**Traditional Reading:** Greek literally reads "a spirit of Python" — the Python was the serpent associated with the Delphic oracle and the god Apollo. Ellicott notes that "the people of Philippi spoke of the maiden" this way, and Luke "recognised in her phenomena identical with those of the priestesses of Delphi, the wild distortions, the shrill cries, the madness of an evil inspiration." She brought her masters much profit through fortune-telling (Greek: *manteuomene*, "soothsaying" as distinct from genuine prophecy). The demon cried out truthfully — "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim…the way of salvation" — but Paul wanted no demonic endorsement.
— studylight.org (Ellicott), enduringword.com (quoting Boice)

### v. 18 — Paul casts out the spirit

**Traditional Reading:** After "many days" of this, Paul became "greatly annoyed" (Greek: *diaponeomai*, a strong term of vexation). He turned and commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out — and it left "at that very moment" (Bruce: "there and then"). Guzik notes: "Paul knew that a man will be identified by both his friends and his enemies, and could do without a demonic letter of reference."
— enduringword.com, studylight.org (Gill)

### vv. 19–21 — Paul and Silas dragged before magistrates

**Traditional Reading:** The owners' real grievance was financial — "their hope of profit was gone" — but they framed it as a civic and ethnic issue. They accused Paul and Silas of being Jews disturbing the city and promoting customs unlawful for Romans. Anti-Jewish sentiment lay near the surface in the ancient world (Bruce). Notably, Luke (a Gentile) and Timothy (half-Greek) were not seized — only the obviously Jewish Paul and Silas.
— enduringword.com (quoting Bruce)

### vv. 22–24 — Beaten and imprisoned

**Traditional Reading:** Without trial, the magistrates had them stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the "inner prison" with feet fastened in stocks. The Romans had no limit on the number of stripes (unlike the Jewish 39 lashes). Paul later wrote of "stripes above measure" (2 Cor. 11:23). The stocks likely had multiple holes to force the legs apart, causing "the utmost discomfort and cramping pain" (Bruce). Tertullian later commented: "The legs feel nothing in the stocks when the heart is in heaven."
— enduringword.com

### v. 25 — Praying and singing at midnight

**Traditional Reading:** Despite their wounds, Paul and Silas were "praying and singing hymns to God" — not quietly but audibly, since "the prisoners were listening." Stott: "Instead of cursing men, they blessed God." Guzik notes that "anyone can be happy in pleasant circumstances, but real joy comes only from within."
— enduringword.com

### v. 26 — The earthquake

**Traditional Reading:** The earthquake was clearly supernatural: not only in its timing but because "all the doors flew open and everyone's chains came loose" — yet no one was crushed and no one escaped.
— enduringword.com

### vv. 27–29 — The jailer prevented from suicide

**Traditional Reading:** Waking to find doors open, the jailer assumed prisoners had fled and drew his sword to kill himself — Roman military law held a guard liable with his own life for escaped prisoners (cf. Acts 12:19). Paul's cry, "Do not harm yourself! We are all here!" saved his life. The jailer called for lights, rushed in trembling, and fell before Paul and Silas. The prisoners had stayed — a testimony to Paul's spiritual authority even among criminals.
— enduringword.com

### vv. 30–31 — "What must I do to be saved?" / "Believe in the Lord Jesus"

**Traditional Reading:** The jailer's question and Paul's answer form one of the simplest and clearest gospel presentations in Scripture. The answer is not "be baptised," "keep the law," or "join the church," but "Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household."

**Denominational Differences — The relationship of faith to baptism (v. 31 in context with v. 33):**

- **Baptist:** John MacArthur (GTY) cites this verse as proof that salvation is by faith alone, not by baptism. The jailer was told to *believe*; baptism followed (v. 33) as an act of obedience, not as a cause of salvation. This is the classic Baptist reading: "Believe…and you will be saved" is the gospel; baptism testifies to it.
  — gty.org

- **Lutheran:** Lutherans agree salvation is by faith alone (*sola fide*), but insist that baptism is a means by which God creates and strengthens that faith. The jailer's household heard the Word (v. 32), believed, and were baptised — the Word and sacrament working together. Luther's Small Catechism says baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe this."
  — 1517.org

- **Reformed / Presbyterian:** Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, not the instrument of regeneration itself. The Spirit works when and where He wills, ordinarily through the means of grace (Word and sacrament), but the sacrament does not automatically regenerate. The jailer believed, then was baptised. The promise is "to you and your household" — language consistent with covenant theology.
  — ligonier.org

— enduringword.com, gty.org, 1517.org, ligonier.org

### v. 32 — The Word of the Lord spoken to the household

**Traditional Reading:** Paul and Silas "spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house." This preaching preceded baptism (v. 33). The household had to hear and understand the gospel.
— enduringword.com

### vv. 33–34 — Washing wounds, baptism, and a meal

**Traditional Reading:** The jailer's conversion produced immediate fruit: he washed their wounds (the same jailer who had earlier fastened them in stocks), he and his whole household were baptised "without delay" (at that hour of the night), he set a meal before them, and he rejoiced "having believed in God with all his household." The order is: hearing the Word → believing → baptism → rejoicing.
— enduringword.com

**Debated Modern Teaching — "Household salvation":** Some Word of Faith and charismatic teachers have used v. 31 ("you and your household") to teach that if the head of a household believes, the whole household is automatically saved. The traditional reading across all major traditions is that each person must personally believe — v. 32 shows the Word was spoken to *everyone* in the house, and v. 34 says "he and all his household rejoiced that *they had come to believe* in God." The promise is that the way of salvation is open to the whole household, not that one person's faith saves the rest.
— (This point was not found on the specified sites but is widely noted in evangelical commentary; the text of vv. 32, 34 makes the point internally.)

### vv. 35–36 — Magistrates order release

**Traditional Reading:** The magistrates, perhaps shaken by the earthquake or simply thinking a beating and a night in prison was sufficient, sent officers (lictors, rod-bearers) to order their release. The jailer relayed the news with relief.
— enduringword.com

### vv. 37–39 — Paul claims his Roman citizenship

**Traditional Reading:** Paul now reveals he and Silas are Roman citizens. They had been beaten publicly without trial — a grave violation of Roman law (the *Lex Porcia* and *Lex Julia* forbade beating a Roman citizen without due process). Paul insists the magistrates come personally to escort them out, not to exact revenge but to publicly establish the innocence of the church in Philippi and to protect the fledgling congregation from future harassment. When the magistrates heard "Roman citizens," they were "alarmed" — they themselves could face severe penalties for this illegality. They came and "appeased" (or "entreated") them, escorting them out while requesting they leave the city.
— enduringword.com

### v. 40 — Farewell to Lydia and the brothers

**Traditional Reading:** On their own terms, Paul and Silas went to Lydia's house (now the meeting-place of the Philippian church), saw "the brothers" (the first mention of a formal group of believers in Philippi), encouraged them, and departed — leaving behind what would become one of Paul's most beloved churches (see the Epistle to the Philippians).
— enduringword.com

---

### Summary of Major Protestant Differences in Acts 16

| Issue | Baptist | Reformed/Presbyterian | Lutheran | Wesleyan/Methodist |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **v. 14 "the Lord opened her heart"** | God sovereignly opens hearts; monergistic regeneration | Same: effectual calling precedes faith | God works through the Word preached to open hearts | Prevenient grace enables free response; Lydia was already seeking |
| **v. 15, 33 household baptisms** | Not infant baptism; all who were baptised believed first | Consistent with covenant infant baptism, though not proving it | Baptism as means of grace, regenerating infants who believe | Baptism as sign of new birth; infants may be baptised (covenant) |
| **v. 31 "Believe...and you will be saved"** | Faith alone; baptism follows as obedience | Faith alone; baptism as sign and seal of faith | Faith alone, yet baptism is a means by which God gives faith | Faith alone; baptism as outward sign of inward grace |

**Sources used:** enduringword.com (Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic evangelical), preceptaustin.org (evangelical), studylight.org/geb (Gill/Baptist), studylight.org/ebc (Ellicott/Anglican), gty.org (MacArthur/Baptist), ligonier.org (Reformed), 1517.org (Lutheran), thegospelcoalition.org (Reformed-Baptist evangelical).
